name: Z → μ⁺μ⁻
explanation: The Z couples a fermion to its own antiparticle, so a Z can decay into a μ⁺μ⁻ pair. This leptonic mode is about 3.4 % of all Z decays. Each charged lepton family gives the same fraction, which tests lepton universality.

name: μ⁻ → e⁻ ν̄_e ν_μ
explanation: The muon decays through a virtual W⁻: it turns into a ν_μ and the W⁻ becomes an electron and an electron antineutrino. Each lepton family number is conserved separately. This accounts for essentially all muon decays.

name: t → b W⁺
explanation: The top quark is heavy enough to decay into a real W⁺ and a b quark, so no virtual W is needed. The coupling is |V_tb|, which is very close to 1. The top therefore decays almost entirely this way, in about 5 × 10⁻²⁵ s, before it can form hadrons.

name: H → b b̄
explanation: The Higgs couples to fermions in proportion to their mass, and the b quark is the heaviest fermion that a 125 GeV Higgs can decay into. The coupling is the b-quark Yukawa coupling. This makes H → b b̄ the largest Higgs decay mode.

name: π⁺ → μ⁺ ν_μ
explanation: The u and d̄ in the π⁺ annihilate into a virtual W⁺, which becomes a μ⁺ and a ν_μ. The π⁺ has spin 0, so the V−A weak current produces the lepton pair with fixed helicities, which favors the heavier lepton. That is why this mode dominates over π⁺ → e⁺ν_e.

name: n → p e⁻ ν̄_e
explanation: A d quark in the neutron turns into a u quark by emitting a W⁻, which becomes an electron and an electron antineutrino. The other two quarks are spectators and join the new u to make a proton. Very little energy is released, so the neutron lives about 15 minutes.

name: J/ψ → μ⁺ μ⁻
explanation: The c c̄ pair in the J/ψ annihilates into a virtual photon, which makes a μ⁺μ⁻ pair. This electromagnetic decay needs no gluons to rearrange quarks, so it competes well with the OZI-suppressed hadronic modes. It is the reference for J/ψ → π⁺π⁻π⁰.

name: τ⁻ → π⁻ ν_τ
explanation: The τ⁻ emits a virtual W⁻ that becomes a d ū pair, which forms the π⁻. The W couples to the u–d current with |V_ud| of about 0.97. This makes τ⁻ → π⁻ν_τ about 11 % of all τ decays.

name: K⁺ → μ⁺ ν_μ
explanation: The u and s̄ annihilate into a virtual W⁺ that decays to μ⁺ν_μ; the s → u coupling costs a factor |V_us| of about 0.22. It is still the largest K⁺ decay mode, so it is the reference for the suppressed K⁺ decays. The heavier muon is favored over the electron by helicity.

name: ρ⁰ → π⁺ π⁻
explanation: The ρ⁰ is built from u ū (or d d̄); a gluon makes a d d̄ pair out of the vacuum and the quarks regroup into a π⁺ and a π⁻. This strong decay conserves everything and is very fast, with a width of about 150 MeV. It is essentially the only decay of the ρ⁰.

name: K*⁺ → K⁰ π⁺
explanation: A u quark in the K*⁺ (u s̄) emits a gluon that makes a d d̄ pair, and the quarks regroup into a π⁺ (u d̄) and a K⁰ (d s̄). This strong decay is fast, with a width of about 51 MeV. Isospin fixes the split: K⁰π⁺ is two thirds and K⁺π⁰ one third of the decays.

name: φ → K⁺ K⁻
explanation: The s s̄ pair in the φ creates a u ū pair through a gluon, and the quarks regroup into a K⁻ (s ū) and a K⁺ (u s̄). The strange quark lines run straight from the φ into the kaons, so this decay is not OZI-suppressed. It is just above threshold, so the φ is narrow, with a width of about 4 MeV.

name: Σ⁰ → Λ γ
explanation: The Σ⁰ and the Λ have the same quark content (u d s) and differ only in isospin and spin structure, which the diagram cannot show. A quark in the Σ⁰ emits a photon, so this is an electromagnetic transition. It is the only way for the Σ⁰ to decay, so its lifetime is only about 7 × 10⁻²⁰ s.

name: K_S → π⁺ π⁻
explanation: The s̄ in the K⁰ turns into a ū by emitting a W⁺ that becomes u d̄, and the spectator d joins the ū to form the π⁻. A weak ΔS = 1 decay like this is slow compared with strong decays, so the K_S lives about 90 ps. It is the main K_S decay mode, about 69 %.

name: Λ → p π⁻
explanation: The strange quark in the Λ turns into a u quark by emitting a W⁻ that becomes a d ū pair, which forms the π⁻. The spectator u and d join the new u to make a proton. This weak ΔS = 1 decay pays |V_us| but is still the main Λ decay, about two thirds of the total.

name: Δ⁺⁺ → p π⁺
explanation: One of the three u quarks in the Δ⁺⁺ emits a gluon that makes a d d̄ pair, and the quarks regroup into a proton (u u d) and a π⁺ (u d̄). This strong decay is very fast, with a width of about 117 MeV. It is essentially the only decay channel of the Δ⁺⁺.

name: D⁰ → K⁻ π⁺
explanation: The charm quark turns into a strange quark by emitting a W⁺ that becomes u d̄, forming the π⁺, and the strange quark joins the spectator ū in the K⁻. Both weak vertices use large CKM elements, V_cs and V_ud, so this Cabibbo-favored mode is the standard reference for D⁰ decays.

name: B̄⁰ → D⁺ π⁻
explanation: The b quark turns into a c quark by emitting a W⁻ that becomes d ū, which forms the π⁻, and the c quark joins the spectator d̄ in the D⁺. The W goes into a different meson than the b-quark remnants, so no color matching between hadrons is needed. This color-allowed b → c decay is the reference for the suppressed B̄⁰ decays.

decay.brText: (2.51 ± 0.08) × 10⁻³ (CP conjugate of the PDG B⁰ → D⁻π⁺)

name: B⁰ → D⁻ π⁺
explanation: The b̄ in the B⁰ turns into a c̄ by emitting a W⁺ that becomes u d̄, forming the π⁺, and the c̄ joins the spectator d in the D⁻. It is the antiparticle twin (CP conjugate) of B̄⁰ → D⁺π⁻ and has the same branching ratio. It uses the dominant b → c transition.

name: B_s → D_s⁻ π⁺
explanation: The b̄ in the B_s turns into a c̄ by emitting a W⁺ that becomes u d̄, forming the π⁺, and the c̄ joins the spectator s in the D_s⁻. This is the B_s analogue of B⁰ → D⁻π⁺ and a standard b → c reference decay.

name: K_L → π⁻ e⁺ ν_e
explanation: As in K_S decay, the s̄ turns into a ū by emitting a W⁺, but now the W⁺ becomes a positron and an electron neutrino. The spectator d joins the ū to form the π⁻. Semileptonic decays like this make up most K_L decays, because the two-pion decay is almost forbidden by CP symmetry.

decay.brText: (40.55 ± 0.11) % for π±e∓ν; the π⁻e⁺ν_e mode is half of that

name: K⁺ → π⁰ e⁺ ν_e
explanation: The s̄ in the K⁺ turns into a ū by emitting a W⁺ that becomes e⁺ν_e, and the ū joins the spectator u in the π⁰. The s → u transition costs a factor |V_us|. With three particles in the final state there is no helicity suppression, so this reaches about 5 %.

name: ω → π⁺ π⁻ π⁰
explanation: The ω is mostly (u ū + d d̄); one gluon creates a d d̄ pair and a second gluon a u ū pair, so the quark lines stay connected and three pions emerge. G-parity forbids two pions but allows three, which makes this the dominant ω decay at about 89 %. It is the reference for ω → π⁺π⁻.

name: π⁰ → γ γ
explanation: The u ū (or d d̄) pair in the π⁰ annihilates into two photons by exchanging a quark. This electromagnetic decay is the main π⁰ mode, about 99 % of all decays, with a lifetime of only about 8 × 10⁻¹⁷ s. The deeper field-theory origin of the rate is the quark triangle anomaly, which this tree-level picture does not show.
